sections.title: Four photos and a diplomatic row
sections.intro_md:
On **2 and 3 January 2024**, Prime Minister Narendra Modi spent a day in Lakshadweep, opening a solar plant and an undersea internet cable. Then he posted holiday-style pictures: snorkelling over coral, walking a white beach at dawn, sitting in a beach chair.

The pictures did something the territory's tourism office had never managed. Indians started comparing the islands with the **Maldives**, 125 km to the south. Three Maldivian deputy ministers mocked the posts, were **suspended on 7 January**, and #BoycottMaldives trended in India. Indian arrivals in the Maldives fell **42%** in the first four months of 2024.

Here is the paradox. The place a country suddenly wanted to visit has **32 km² of land**, less than a tenth of Chennai's city area, one short runway, and a rule that **every visitor needs a permit**. In 2018 it received about **10,400 domestic tourists in a whole year**. Agatti airport then went from **47,266 passengers** in 2023 to 24 to **117,409** the next year.

This day is about what those photos did not show: a sea people of Malayali and Maldivian descent, nearly all Muslim, where houses pass through mothers, men once lived from the sea and coconut, and India keeps an eye on the busiest shipping lanes of the Arabian Sea.

spotlights.name: The January 2024 visit
spotlights.spot_it: A leader in a snorkel mask, a turquoise lagoon, and a hashtag war with the Maldives.
spotlights.story_md: Modi's visit was official business: a **solar power plant** in Kavaratti and the opening of an **undersea fibre-optic cable** from Kochi to the islands, inaugurated in January 2024. The photos he posted on **4 January** were the bit that travelled. A Maldivian politician mocked them; three deputy ministers posted insults about Indians; the Maldives government **suspended all three on 7 January** and said they spoke for themselves. India summoned the Maldivian envoy on **8 January**. Travel companies ran Lakshadweep campaigns within days. The row also had a hard edge: President **Mohamed Muizzu** had won office in 2023 asking Indian military personnel to leave, and the last of them did on **10 May 2024**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a little-known territory into a national talking point overnight.
spotlights.memory_hook: One snorkel, one hashtag, 42% fewer Indians in the Maldives.

spotlights.name: The lagoons
spotlights.when: Formed over the last few thousand years on far older reef
spotlights.spot_it: Water in three bands: pale green over sand, electric blue over the shallows, ink-blue past the reef edge.
spotlights.story_md: The colour in the photos is a physics lesson. Inside each atoll ring the water is often **under 4 metres deep** over white coral sand, so sunlight bounces back and the water glows turquoise. Past the reef crest the sea floor drops away to hundreds of metres within a short swim, and the water turns deep blue. Lakshadweep's **lagoons cover about 4,200 km²**, more than **125 times** the area of its land. That is why islanders think of the lagoon, not the island, as their home ground: it is where the bait fish for tuna are caught, where children learn to swim, and where boats shelter from the monsoon.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The islands are the thin rim; the lagoon is the real territory.
spotlights.memory_hook: 32 km² of land, 4,200 km² of lagoon: the frame is bigger than the picture.

sections.title: The territory at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Lakshadweep is **India's smallest union territory**: **32.62 km²** of land spread over **36 islands and islets**, of which only **10 are inhabited**. Its islands lie **200 to 440 km off the Kerala coast**, in three groups: the **Amindivi** islands in the north, the **Laccadive** islands in the middle, and **Minicoy** alone in the south, across the Nine Degree Channel.

The land is tiny but the sea is not. The territory holds about **4,200 km² of lagoons** and an **exclusive economic zone of about 400,000 km²**, roughly a fifth of India's total, which is why fisheries and the Navy care about it.

In 2011 it had **64,473 people**, packed at **1,976 per km²**. About **96.6% are Muslim**, about **95% are recognised as Scheduled Tribes**, and **78%** live in places the census calls urban. It is run by an **Administrator** appointed by the President, has **one Lok Sabha seat**, no legislature, and falls under the **Kerala High Court**. The capital is **Kavaratti**.

spotlights.name: Kavaratti
spotlights.spot_it: A 5.8 km sliver of coconut palms with a lagoon on the west, a lighthouse, and dozens of small white mosques.
spotlights.story_md: Kavaratti covers **4.22 km²** and had **11,210 people** in 2011, at nearly **2,920 per km²**. It became the seat of the Administrator only in **1964**; before that the islands were run from **Kozhikode** on the mainland. The first bank branch arrived in **1971**. In **2005** it got the world's first **low-temperature thermal desalination** plant, which turns sea water into drinking water using the cold of the deep ocean. Tourism material counts **52 mosques** on the island, the best known being the carved Ujra mosque. The **INS Dweeprakshak** naval base sits here too.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where every decision for the islands is made and where most ships call first.
spotlights.memory_hook: A capital you can walk end to end before lunch.

spotlights.name: A hundred thousand islands
spotlights.spot_it: Seen from space: a scatter of pale green rings on a dark blue sea, west of Kerala.
spotlights.story_md: **Lakshadweep** means 'a hundred thousand islands' in Sanskrit and Malayalam: *laksha* (one lakh) plus *dweep* (island). The count is poetic; there are 36. The Greek geographer **Ptolemy**, in the 2nd century CE, listed **1,378 islands** in these waters. Until **1973** the territory had a clumsy official name, the **Laccadive, Minicoy and Amindivi Islands**, from the three groups merged in **1956**. It was renamed Lakshadweep on **1 November 1973**. The old English word 'Laccadive' survives in sea charts as the **Laccadive Sea**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The name reaches for the whole chain of atolls, including the Maldives, not just India's slice.
spotlights.memory_hook: A lakh of islands promised, thirty-six delivered.

sections.title: How a ring of coral becomes an island
sections.intro_md:
Every island here is made of **coral**, the limestone skeletons of tiny animals, stacked on top of a sunken volcanic ridge. The **Chagos-Laccadive Ridge** runs about **2,550 km** north to south under the Indian Ocean; Lakshadweep is its northern tip, the Maldives its middle and the Chagos Islands its southern end. The rock below formed around the time India broke away from Madagascar and the Seychelles, close to **66 million years ago**.

On top of that sinking base, reefs kept growing upward toward the light. The result is the **atoll**: a ring of reef around a lagoon, with low islands of broken coral and sand piled on the rim by storms. Lakshadweep has **12 atolls, 3 reefs and 5 submerged banks**. No island is more than about **1.6 km wide**, and most land stands **1 to 2 metres** above high tide.

That makes the islands fragile. **Parali I**, an islet of Bangaram atoll, had **disappeared by 2017**, and studies the same year found erosion on several others. Fresh water lives in a thin **lens** floating on salt water under each island, refilled only by monsoon rain, about **1,600 mm** a year.

spotlights.name: The atoll
spotlights.spot_it: A ring of reef, white surf on the outside, a calm lagoon inside, palm-covered islands on one edge.
spotlights.story_md: A coral atoll starts as a **fringing reef** around a volcanic island. As the island slowly sinks, the coral keeps building upward, because the animals need sunlight. Over hundreds of thousands of years the volcano disappears below the surface and only the ring of reef remains, enclosing a lagoon. **Charles Darwin** worked this out in **1842** from his Beagle voyage, before anyone could test it. Drilling on **Enewetak** in the Pacific later found volcanic basalt about **1,400 metres** below the coral. The world has roughly **440 atolls**; Lakshadweep and the Maldives hold a large share of the Indian Ocean's.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why the islands are low, ring-shaped and always on one side of a lagoon.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sunken volcano wearing a crown of coral.

spotlights.name: Andrott
spotlights.when: First island to accept Islam, by tradition
spotlights.spot_it: The one island that is not on an atoll ring: long, fat and close to the mainland, with no proper lagoon.
spotlights.story_md: **Andrott** is the largest island at **4.98 km²**, and with about **11,000 people** one of the two most populous. It is also the **nearest to the mainland**, about **293 km** from Kochi. Unlike most of its neighbours it has almost no lagoon, which makes landing boats harder. By local tradition it was the **first island to embrace Islam**, and its Juma mosque holds the tomb of **Ubaidullah**, the saint said to have brought the faith in **661 CE**. It also has **Buddhist remains**, a sign of what came before. Old French maps called it **Divanduru**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It anchors the territory's religious history.
spotlights.memory_hook: Biggest island, closest to Kerala, oldest Muslim memory.

spotlights.name: Bitra
spotlights.spot_it: A dot of sand and palms, smaller than a large park, on the rim of a 54 km² lagoon.
spotlights.story_md: Bitra is the **smallest inhabited island**: **0.177 km²**, about the size of 25 football pitches, with a highest point of **2 metres**. In 2011 it had **271 people**. For centuries islanders from Kiltan and Chetlat only visited to **collect seabird eggs**. Nobody lived there until **1945**, when **a woman from Chetlat** made it her home. It has a shrine to **Malik Mulla**, an Arab saint said to be buried there, and was the **last island to get electricity**, in **1982**. In **2025** the Administration floated a proposal to take over the island for defence use, which residents opposed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how recent and fragile settlement can be on the smallest atolls.
spotlights.memory_hook: Settled by one woman in 1945, eyed by the defence planners in 2025.

spotlights.name: Parali I, the island that vanished
spotlights.spot_it: Look for it on old maps of Bangaram atoll; on the reef today there is only shallow water.
spotlights.story_md: Bangaram atoll had five islets. The smallest, **Parali I**, was a low bank of sand and rubble with a few plants. By **2017** it had been **completely washed away**. A study published that year measured erosion on the others too: **Parali II had lost about 80%** of its area, **Thinnakara 14.4%**, **Parali III 11.4%** and **Bangaram 9.9%**. The causes are argued over: rising sea level, stronger storms, changes in currents, and the damage done to reefs that once broke the waves. Whatever the mix, the islets here are made of loose sand and rubble, and they move.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest warning of what climate change can mean for a territory built 1 to 2 metres above the sea.
spotlights.memory_hook: An island on the map, a sandbar in the 2000s, open sea by 2017.

spotlights.name: Kalpeni and its storm bank
spotlights.spot_it: A long island with a wall of grey coral rubble along its eastern shore and small islets dotted in the lagoon.
spotlights.story_md: Kalpeni atoll (**3.08 km²**, lagoon about **25.6 km²**) is about **287 km** west of Kochi. Along its eastern and southern shores lies a ridge of **coral debris** thrown up by a violent **storm in 1847**, which still acts as a sea wall. The atoll has small islets with their own names: **Cheriyam** to the north, the **Tilakkam** group, and **Pitti**, just **3.6 hectares**, a favourite snorkelling spot. Archaeological finds on Kalpeni suggest people were here by about **1500 BCE**, the earliest evidence for the whole archipelago.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how one storm can rebuild an island's shape for centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: A storm in 1847 built Kalpeni's sea wall for free.

sections.title: Life on the reef
sections.intro_md:
The islands have **no forests** and about **400 kinds of flowering plants**, mostly coconut. The life is in the water. Surveys list over **600 species of marine fish**, **78 of coral**, **82 of seaweed**, **52 of crabs** and three seagrasses, plus whales and dolphins in the deep water just off the reefs. On land, **101 bird species** have been recorded, many of them seabirds that nest on uninhabited islets.

The territory's official animal is a reef fish, the **butterfly fish**, and its official bird is the **sooty tern**. Both depend on healthy coral and quiet islands, and both have had a hard few decades. Warm-water events in **1998, 2010, 2016 and 2024** bleached Lakshadweep's reefs, and seabird colonies have shrunk as people and boats reached remote islets.

The territory has answered with protected areas: the **Pitti** bird island, a **marine birds reserve** named after the MP P. M. Sayeed, and in **2020** the world's first reserve made just for **sea cucumbers**.

visual.title: Who lives on a Lakshadweep reef

spotlights.name: Butterfly fish (state animal)
spotlights.spot_it: A flat, yellow-and-white oval fish with two dark saddle marks on the back and a black bar through the eye.
spotlights.story_md: The **blackwedged butterflyfish**, *Chaetodon falcula*, is Lakshadweep's state animal. It is about the size of a hand, lives in pairs on coral reefs of the Indian Ocean, and picks at coral polyps and small invertebrates with a pointed mouth. The black stripe through the eye and a dark spot near the tail are thought to confuse predators about which end is the head. Because butterflyfish feed on coral, divers and scientists use them as a quick health check: **where butterflyfish vanish, the coral is usually in trouble**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living gauge of reef health, chosen as the face of the territory.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fish that wears a fake eye near its tail.

spotlights.name: Sooty tern (state bird)
spotlights.spot_it: A slim seabird, black above and white below, with a forked tail and a loud 'wide-a-wake' call.
spotlights.story_md: The sooty tern is the territory's state bird and the reason **Pitti**, a sandbank about **24 km north of Kavaratti**, is a protected bird island. Sooty terns breed in dense colonies on bare coral islands and lay **a single egg** in a scrape on the ground. Their feathers have so little oil that they **cannot float**, so a young bird that leaves the colony may stay **on the wing for 3 to 10 years** before returning to land to breed. Islanders once sailed to Pitti and other islets to collect tern eggs, a practice now banned.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ties the territory's identity to its most remote, uninhabited islets.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bird that cannot land on water and does not need to for a decade.

spotlights.name: Green turtles in the seagrass
spotlights.spot_it: A big olive-brown turtle grazing head-down in a meadow of green seagrass in shallow water.
spotlights.story_md: Four species of sea turtle are reported in Lakshadweep: **green, hawksbill, olive ridley and leatherback**. Green turtles are the ones a snorkeller meets most, grazing on the **seagrass beds** that cover about **13.8 km²** at Kadmat alone. Adult green turtles are almost entirely **vegetarian**, which is unusual among sea turtles, and the fat under their shell is tinted green by their diet, which gives them their name. Marine biologists working at Agatti and Kadmat have recorded rising turtle numbers, and in some lagoons the grazing is now heavy enough to thin the seagrass.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a protection success that is reshaping the lagoon floor.
spotlights.memory_hook: Named for the colour of its fat, not its shell.

spotlights.name: The sea cucumber reserve
spotlights.spot_it: A soft, sausage-shaped animal lying on sand, often dusted with it, that looks more like a vegetable than an animal.
spotlights.story_md: Sea cucumbers are relatives of starfish that vacuum the sea floor, eating sand and passing it out cleaner. Dried, they are a luxury food in East Asia, sold for up to about **USD 1,000 a kilo**. India banned their harvest in **2001**, but poachers kept taking them from Lakshadweep's reefs. In **2020** the government declared the **Dr K. K. Mohammed Koya Sea Cucumber Conservation Reserve**, on the uninhabited **Cheriyapani** reef in the north, the **first protected area in the world set up for sea cucumbers**. It is named after a local marine scientist.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rare case of India writing a global first in marine protection.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's first nature reserve for an animal that eats sand.

spotlights.name: Coral bleaching
spotlights.spot_it: Coral that has turned bone-white, still standing but with its colour gone.
spotlights.story_md: Reef-building corals live with tiny algae inside their tissue that feed them sugar and give them colour. When the sea stays about **1 °C above its normal summer peak** for weeks, the partnership breaks down and the coral expels the algae, turning white. If the heat lasts, it starves. The **1998** El Nino hit Lakshadweep hard; surveys afterwards reported that live coral cover at many sites fell by **roughly half or more**. Reefs recovered over the next decade, then bleached again in **2010**, **2016** and in the global event of **2024**. Each time, the gap for recovery gets shorter.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The reefs are the islands' sea wall and fish nursery; when they die, both go.
spotlights.memory_hook: White coral is not dead yet, it is starving.

spotlights.name: Reef manta rays
spotlights.when: Seen year round off the reef edge
spotlights.spot_it: A huge flat black-and-white ray, wider than a person is tall, gliding with its mouth open.
spotlights.story_md: The **reef manta ray** can span **3 to 5 metres** from wingtip to wingtip and filters plankton from the water. Lakshadweep lists **manta rays** among its notable marine animals, along with sharks, tunas, flying fish and octopus. Divers at Kadmat and Agatti see them at cleaning stations, where small fish pick parasites off their skin. Mantas have one of the largest brains relative to body size of any fish, and in tests in aquariums they appear to recognise their own reflection.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the animal most divers come for, and a reason for the territory to keep its reefs clean.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fish the width of a car that stops at a car wash.

sections.title: Sailors, saints and a queen in Kannur
sections.intro_md:
People reached these islands early. Finds on **Kalpeni** point to settlement by about **1500 BCE**. The islands appear in Buddhist **Jataka** tales, in the Tamil Sangam poems, and in the Greek sailing guide **Periplus of the Erythraean Sea** in the 1st century CE, because they sat on the sea route from Arabia to Sri Lanka and beyond.

The mainland powers of south India each claimed them in turn. The **Pallavas** took them in the late 7th century after a naval battle, the **Cholas** under **Rajendra I** in **1018 to 1019**, and later the kings of **Kannur**. Islam came, by tradition, in **661 CE**; the first settlers are said to have been Hindus from Kerala, which is why caste-like ranks and **matrilineal** families survive among the Muslim islanders today.

From the 16th century the islands belonged in practice to the **Arakkal** family of Kannur, Kerala's only Muslim royal house. **Tipu Sultan** took the northern islands in **1787**, the **British** took them in **1799**, and the rest followed in **1908**. Independent India made them a union territory on **1 November 1956**.

spotlights.name: Ubaidullah and the coming of Islam
spotlights.spot_it: A whitewashed mosque on Andrott with a saint's tomb inside, visited by islanders from every atoll.
spotlights.story_md: Island tradition says an Arab preacher, **Ubaidullah**, was shipwrecked on the islands in **661 CE** while sailing from Mecca. He began preaching on **Amini**, met hostility, moved on, and finally won converts on **Andrott**, where he died and was buried in the **Juma mosque**. Historians treat the date with care: there is no record from the 7th century, and Islam more likely spread gradually with Arab and Malabar traders over several centuries. What is certain is how deeply the story is held. Ubaidullah's tomb is the most revered shrine in Lakshadweep.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the founding story of the islands' faith.
spotlights.memory_hook: A shipwreck in 661, a tomb on Andrott, a faith across 36 islands.

spotlights.name: Rajendra Chola's island raid
spotlights.spot_it: On the walls of Chola temples: Tamil inscriptions boasting of 'the ancient islands of the sea numbering 12,000'.
spotlights.story_md: The great Tamil emperor **Rajendra Chola I** (ruled 1014 to 1044) ran one of the few medieval Indian navies that crossed open sea. His inscriptions at **Thanjavur** record the capture of the 'old islands of the sea, numbering **12,000**', which historians read as the **Maldives and Lakshadweep**. The islands mattered because they sat on the route of the Arab and Chinese ships whose trade the Cholas wanted to control. After the Cholas, the islands passed to a small Hindu kingdom and then, in the early 12th century, to the kings of Kannur.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the first solid evidence of an Indian empire ruling these islands.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rajendra counted 12,000 islands; Lakshadweep has 36.

spotlights.name: The Arakkal rulers
spotlights.spot_it: A whitewashed palace by the Kannur shore, now a museum; its rulers were often women called Arakkal Beevi.
spotlights.story_md: The **Arakkal** family of **Kannur** was the only Muslim royal house of Kerala. Its rulers inherited through the **female line**, so the eldest member, man or woman, ruled; the women were called **Arakkal Beevi**. In the 16th century the **Kolathiri** kings granted them the islands, partly to protect them from the **Portuguese**, whom the islanders had already **driven out in 1545**. The Arakkals controlled the islands' **coir** trade tightly. In **1905** the last Ali Raja gave up his rights for a pension, and the palace's Durbar Hall in Kannur became a **museum in 2005**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: For three centuries the islands' lords were a matrilineal Muslim dynasty on the mainland.
spotlights.memory_hook: The islands answered to a queen in Kannur.

spotlights.name: Tipu Sultan takes the northern islands
spotlights.spot_it: The Mysore ruler in green and gold in his portraits; on the map, the five northern islands of Amini, Kadmat, Kiltan, Chetlat and Bitra.
spotlights.story_md: In **1787** the islanders of the northern **Amindivi** group, tired of the Arakkal coir monopoly, asked **Tipu Sultan** of Mysore to take them over, and he did. So for twelve years the northern islands answered to Srirangapatna while the rest stayed with Kannur. When Tipu died fighting the British in **1799**, the Amindivi islands passed to the **East India Company**. The rest stayed with the Arakkals, who paid tribute to the British until **1908**, when the British took over citing unpaid taxes and joined all the islands to the **Madras Presidency**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why the north and south of the territory were run differently for over a century.
spotlights.memory_hook: The northern islands chose Tipu over the Kannur coir bosses.

sections.title: Minicoy, the island that faces south
sections.intro_md:
**Minicoy** is the odd one out. It sits alone **201 km south of Kalpeni**, across the Nine Degree Channel, and only **125 km north of Thuraakunu**, the northernmost island of the Maldives. Its people call it **Maliku** and speak **Dhivehi**, the language of the Maldives, written in the Maldivian **Thaana** script. Their food, dress, songs and boats are Maldivian in style.

Until the 16th century Minicoy was part of the Maldivian world; old Maldivian royal decrees called the king sovereign of everything 'between **Maliku** and **Addu**'. It then passed to the Arakkal rulers of Kannur, and to the British, who made it a lighthouse station on the sea lane from Aden to Colombo.

Minicoy had **10,447 people** in 2011, living in **11 villages** strung along a single island about **10 km long**. Since 1956 direct travel to the Maldives, which you can almost see from the southern tip, has been forbidden. In **2024** the Navy commissioned a base here, and an air base was approved.

spotlights.name: Minicoy (Maliku)
spotlights.spot_it: A crescent island along the east side of a big oval lagoon, with a tall black-and-white lighthouse at the southern end.
spotlights.story_md: Minicoy is the **second largest** and **southernmost** island of Lakshadweep. The atoll is about **10 km long and 6 km wide**; the inhabited island hugs its eastern rim. The name has a comic origin. A British official asked an islander where he was from; the man, who worked in the **Nicobar Islands**, which Minicoy sailors called *Minikaa-raajje*, gave both names, and the official wrote down **'Minikaa'**, later anglicised to **Minicoy**. The language got a similar mix-up: when an islander said 'Mahaldeebu' to explain his speech, it was recorded as **'Mahl'**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's cultural bridge to the Maldives, inside India's borders.
spotlights.memory_hook: An island named after a mishearing, speaking a language named after another.

spotlights.name: Minicoy Lighthouse
spotlights.spot_it: A 49.5 m tower with a red lantern rising far above the coconut palms; its flash comes every 15 seconds.
spotlights.story_md: After the **Suez Canal** opened, ships from Europe to Asia passed close to Minicoy through the **Eight Degree Channel**, and several wrecked on its reef. The British **Board of Trade** began a lighthouse in **1883**, built from **bricks shipped from London**, and lit it on **2 February 1885**. At **49.5 metres** it is still one of India's tallest, visible **74 km** away. It was run from **Colombo** with the lights of Ceylon until India took control; the Indian flag was raised on top on **2 April 1956**. Visitors can climb it for a view of the whole atoll.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first modern lighthouse in the islands and marks Minicoy's place on a world shipping lane.
spotlights.memory_hook: London bricks, a Colombo boss, an Indian flag in 1956.

spotlights.name: The eleven villages and their boats
spotlights.spot_it: Neat lanes of coral-stone houses grouped into villages, each with its own meeting house and its own big rowing boat.
spotlights.story_md: Minicoy's people live in **11 villages** (athiri or avah), from **Kendiparty** in the north to **Bada** in the south. Each village runs its own affairs through elders, owns shared property, and keeps a long **village boat** rowed by dozens of men in races on festival days. Society was ranked into status groups that trace their origin to **two Maldivian princesses** who, by legend, settled the island: landowners and shipowners, captains, and the descendants of crews. Women own the houses, and a married man traditionally moves into his wife's home.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a living version of Maldivian village life on Indian soil.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eleven villages, eleven boats, one island.

spotlights.name: Minicoy's Buddhist past
spotlights.spot_it: Two low mounds of coral-stone rubble in the palm groves; the only finds are worn stones and a broken Buddha head.
spotlights.story_md: Before Islam reached Minicoy around the **12th century**, its people, like the Maldivians, were **Buddhist**. At **Salliballu** there are two mounds of ruins, a **stupa** and a related building, which the **Archaeological Survey of India** examined in the **1980s**. The sites had been badly damaged, but a large, broken **Buddha head** was found buried there. The local name means 'the place of the cross', after a carved 'cross' that was probably a Buddhist **vajra** symbol. Andrott has Buddhist remains too, so the islands' Buddhist chapter was not confined to Minicoy.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the islands' history is older and more varied than their present faith.
spotlights.memory_hook: The 'cross' at Salliballu was probably a thunderbolt.

sections.title: Jeseri, Mahl and two scripts
sections.intro_md:
Lakshadweep's official language is **English**, with **Malayalam** as an additional official language, and schools teach in Malayalam and English. What people speak at home is something else.

On nine islands the home tongue is **Jeseri** (also called *Dweep bhasha*, 'island speech'), a form of **Malayalam** close to the Arabic-flavoured Malayalam of the Mappila Muslims of Malabar. It has its own sounds: initial *ch* becomes *sh*, *p* becomes *f*, *v* becomes *b*. Each island has its own accent, and older people could tell your island from your first sentence.

On Minicoy people speak **Dhivehi**, the national language of the Maldives, which the census records as **Mahl**. It is an **Indo-Aryan** language, related to Sinhala, not to Malayalam. In 2011, **84.2%** of the territory's people gave Malayalam as their mother tongue and **14.4%** Dhivehi.

spotlights.name: Jeseri, the island Malayalam
spotlights.spot_it: Malayalam that sounds a little off to a Kerala ear: 'fennu' for girl, 'sholli' for said.
spotlights.story_md: The name **Jeseri** probably comes from the Arabic *jazari*, 'of the island'. A visitor from Kerala can follow most of it, but notices the shifts: **'pennu'** (girl) becomes **'fennu'**, **'cholli'** (said) becomes **'sholli'**, **'vili'** (call) becomes **'bili'**, and short vowels drop off the front of words, so **'urangi'** (slept) is **'rangi'**. Jeseri has no script of its own. In the past islanders wrote it in **Arabi Malayalam**, Malayalam written with a modified Arabic alphabet, the way Mappila Muslims on the mainland did; today they use the Malayalam script.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the everyday voice of nine islands, and a link to Kerala's Mappila culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Jeseri, a pen becomes a fen.

spotlights.name: Dhivehi and the Thaana script
spotlights.when: Thaana in use since about the 18th century
spotlights.spot_it: Curly letters written right to left with small marks above and below; it looks like Arabic but is not.
spotlights.story_md: Minicoy's Dhivehi is written in **Thaana**, one of the oddest scripts in the world. It runs **right to left** like Arabic, and its vowels are marks above and below the letters. But the first nine of its letters were built from **Arabic numerals**, and the next nine from the old **Indian-style digits** once used in the Maldives. Dhivehi itself is an **Indo-Aryan** language descended from the Prakrit of ancient Sri Lanka, so its deepest relatives are Sinhala, Hindi and Bengali. On Indian soil, Thaana appears mostly on Minicoy, in religious books and signs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It makes Minicoy the only place in India where this Maldivian script lives.
spotlights.memory_hook: An alphabet built partly out of numbers.

sections.title: Islam, matriliny and the visiting husband
sections.intro_md:
Almost everyone born in Lakshadweep is **Muslim**: **96.6%** in 2011, nearly all **Sunni** of the **Shafi'i** school, like the Mappilas of Malabar. Mosques are everywhere; Kavaratti alone is said to have **52**. Religious life runs on the mosque, the **madrasa**, and the **mouloud**, gatherings that sing the praise of the Prophet.

Yet the islands keep a family system older than their Islam. Most families are **matrilineal**: ancestral property and the family name pass from **mother to daughter**, in a house group called a **tarwad**. In the older pattern a husband did not move in with his wife; he **visited her at night** and spent his days with his own mother's family. Anthropologist **Leela Dube** studied this in Kalpeni in the 1960s and showed how islanders split property in two: tarwad land that follows the female line, and self-earned property that follows **Islamic law**.

Society is also ranked, a trace of Kerala's caste order. The islanders' own terms are **Koya, Malmi** and **Melacheri**. All of them are **Scheduled Tribes**: the government defines the tribe as anyone born on the islands to parents born there.

spotlights.name: Ujra mosque, Kavaratti
spotlights.spot_it: A small low mosque with a sloping roof and a famously carved wooden ceiling, and a well in the courtyard.
spotlights.story_md: The **Mohidden** or **Ujra mosque** in north-west Kavaratti dates from the **17th century**. Its ceiling is a mass of carving that islanders say was cut from **a single piece of driftwood**, and its pillars are carved too. A legend says the carver took his pattern from a leaf, and when he tried to copy it again at home, a chip of wood struck his eye and blinded him, so the design could never be repeated. The **well** in the precinct is believed to have **healing water**, and the grave of **Sheikh Mohammad Kasim** inside is a place of pilgrimage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best known piece of religious architecture in the islands.
spotlights.memory_hook: A ceiling from one drift log, a carver blinded for copying it.

spotlights.name: The tarwad and the visiting husband
spotlights.spot_it: A household of sisters, their mother and children under one roof; the husbands arrive after dark.
spotlights.story_md: In the classic island family, a woman stays all her life in her mother's house, the **tarwad**, with her sisters and their children. Her husband keeps his place in **his** mother's tarwad, works and eats there by day, and comes to his wife's house at night. Children belong to the mother's line. This is called **duolocal** residence, and it let men spend months away at sea without leaving wives alone. Islanders square it with Islam by keeping two kinds of property: ancestral land goes down the female line, while property a man earns himself, sometimes called **'Friday property'**, is divided under Islamic law. Younger couples increasingly set up their own homes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the few places where Islam and matriliny have lived together for centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: Married by day to his mother's house, by night to his wife's.

spotlights.name: Koya, Malmi and Melacheri
spotlights.spot_it: Not visible on sight today; historically, who owned the boats, who sailed them, and who climbed the coconut palms.
spotlights.story_md: Islanders traditionally ranked themselves in three groups. The **Koyas**, at the top, owned land and the large sailing boats called *odam* that carried coir and coconuts to the mainland. The **Malmis** (from *muallim*, navigator) were the sailors and pilots. The **Melacheris** climbed the coconut palms, tapped them and worked the land, and paid the Koyas a share. Islanders explain the ranks as the remains of the Hindu caste order their ancestors brought from Kerala. Free schooling, government jobs and the end of the sailing trade have weakened the hierarchy, but marriages still tend to stay within a group.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains the islands' politics and marriages better than religion does.
spotlights.memory_hook: Boat owners, boat sailors, tree climbers.

sections.title: Sticks, shields and songs for the Prophet
sections.intro_md:
Island performance grew out of two worlds: the **Mappila** arts of the Malabar coast and the **Maldivian** music of Minicoy. Almost all of it is done in groups, by men or by women separately, at weddings, at the end of Ramadan, on the Prophet's birthday, and now on Republic Day stages and for tourists.

The best known are **Kolkali**, a stick dance in a circle, and **Parichakali**, a mock fight with shields and swords; both are men's dances. Women's songs centre on weddings: **Oppana**, sung around the bride. Minicoy has its own dance, **Lava**, and drum rhythms that would sound familiar in Male.

Underneath all of it runs devotional song. The **mouloud**, a long Arabic and Malayalam recital of praise for the Prophet, is held in homes and mosques, especially in the month of his birth. There is no professional stage tradition; performers are fishermen, students and clerks, trained by older neighbours.

spotlights.name: Kolkali
spotlights.when: Performed today at festivals and for visitors
spotlights.spot_it: Men in white mundu and coloured shirts moving in a circle, striking short sticks against their partner's in rhythm.
spotlights.story_md: In **Kolkali**, a group of men, often a dozen or more, stand in a circle holding a short stick in each hand. As the song speeds up they turn, step, crouch and strike sticks with the man in front and the man behind, in patterns that tighten and widen the circle. The steps come from **kalaripayattu**, Kerala's martial art, and the dance came to the islands with settlers from Malabar. The songs, in Jeseri and Malayalam, are sung by the dancers themselves, so the tempo rises as they tire.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most widely performed dance in the islands.
spotlights.memory_hook: A circle of men, two sticks each, no misses allowed.

spotlights.name: Parichakali, the shield dance
spotlights.spot_it: Pairs of men facing off with small round shields and blunt swords, clashing on the beat.
spotlights.story_md: **Parichakali** takes its name from *paricha*, a shield. Dancers pair off with a **shield in one hand and a sword or stick in the other**, and act out a duel to song and drum, striking shield on blade in time, ducking and spinning. It is a warrior dance, close to the shield-and-sword display dances of north Malabar, and is usually performed by the same village groups that do Kolkali, often in one programme. Tourist resorts book village troupes from Kalpeni, Kadmat and Agatti to perform on the beach.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It keeps alive the martial side of island culture.
spotlights.memory_hook: Paricha means shield; the dance is a staged duel.

spotlights.name: Lava, Minicoy's dance
spotlights.spot_it: Men in uniform costume dancing in lines to heavy drums and a lead singer, in a Maldivian style.
spotlights.story_md: **Lava** belongs to Minicoy and has no counterpart on the northern islands. Groups of men, dressed alike, dance in rows to **drumming** and a lead singer, the songs in **Dhivehi**. Steps are springy and synchronised, and the rhythm builds to a fast close. It is danced on festival days and at public events, and is one of the clearest signs that Minicoy's culture faces the Maldives, where similar drum dances, like **bodu beru** ('big drum'), are the national sound.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It marks Minicoy's separate cultural identity within the territory.
spotlights.memory_hook: North dances with sticks; Minicoy dances to the big drum.

spotlights.name: Oppana, the wedding song
spotlights.spot_it: Women seated or circling around a bride, clapping in unison while one woman leads the song and the rest answer.
spotlights.story_md: **Oppana** is a **wedding** performance shared by the Mappilas of Kerala and the islanders. A lead singer, usually a woman, sings in Malayalam mixed with Arabic, and a chorus of women and girls **clap and answer** her as they move around the seated **bride**. The songs tease and bless the bride, describe her beauty and the groom's arrival, and are passed on orally. A men's version is sung around the groom. In Lakshadweep, Oppana still happens in homes, not just on stage, because the wedding party is the stage.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the women's art form at the heart of family life.
spotlights.memory_hook: Clap, answer, tease the bride.

spotlights.name: Mouloud, the praise recital
spotlights.when: Especially in Rabi al-Awwal, the Prophet's birth month
spotlights.spot_it: A room of men seated on mats, reading and singing from the same book, with incense and sweets afterwards.
spotlights.story_md: A **mouloud** (mawlid) is a recital of poems in praise of the Prophet Muhammad, sung in Arabic with Malayalam passages. In Lakshadweep it is held in mosques and in homes to mark the Prophet's birthday, to bless a new house, to give thanks after a voyage, or to honour the dead. Families feed everyone afterwards, often with rice, meat curry and sweets. Islanders also hold large gatherings at the shrines of saints, such as **Ubaidullah's tomb** on Andrott. Nearly everyone in the islands grows up hearing these chants.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the musical backbone of island religious life.
spotlights.memory_hook: A song recited for births, houses, voyages and the dead.

sections.title: Tuna, coconut and an octopus fry
sections.intro_md:
Island food rests on two things the islands have in abundance: **tuna** and **coconut**. Almost nothing else grows on coral sand; rice, vegetables, flour and sugar come by ship from Kerala, and when ships stop in the monsoon, the menu shrinks.

The signature ingredient is **mas** or *mass min*, tuna boiled, smoked and sun-dried until it is as hard as wood. It keeps for months without a fridge, the reason it was traded across the Indian Ocean for centuries. Fresh tuna is fried, curried and minced with coconut. **Octopus**, caught by hand on the reef flat at low tide, is a delicacy.

Coconut is everything else: oil to cook in, milk for curries, grated flesh for almost every dish, and sap for a sweet syrup and jaggery. Sweets are a big part of hospitality, from **kilanji** crepes to the dense, sticky **dweep halwa**. There is no alcohol on the inhabited islands, so the drink is **tender coconut**, black tea, or fresh coconut sap called **neera**.

spotlights.name: Mas, the dried tuna
spotlights.spot_it: Hard, dark brown sticks of fish, like small pieces of wood, sold by weight or grated into curries.
spotlights.story_md: To make **mas**, fishermen gut the tuna, take off head and backbone, and cut each fish into **four long fillets**. The pieces are **boiled**, then **smoked** over coconut husk, then **sun-dried** for days until they turn dark and **wood-hard**. Done well, mas keeps for **months** without refrigeration. About **60%** of Lakshadweep's catch has traditionally been dried, much of it into mas, and shipped to Kerala and Sri Lanka. Shaved or pounded, it gives island and Sri Lankan curries a smoky, savoury depth, like Japanese **katsuobushi**, which is made almost the same way.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the islands' oldest export and the flavour of their cooking.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tuna turned into timber, then grated back into food.

spotlights.name: Mas podichathu
spotlights.spot_it: A dry, golden, flaky stir fry of shredded tuna and grated coconut, flecked with curry leaves.
spotlights.story_md: **Mas podichathu** is the islands' everyday side dish. Dried tuna is softened and shredded, or fresh tuna boiled and flaked, then fried with **grated coconut, turmeric, onion, garlic, green chilli and curry leaves** until dry and fragrant. It is eaten with rice or with chapati and keeps for days. The dish is close cousin to the Maldivian **mas huni**, where tuna, coconut, onion and chilli are mixed raw and eaten with flatbread at breakfast. Tourism menus list it as one of the territory's signature foods.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the simplest way to taste the islands at home.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tuna and coconut, fried until they forget which is which.

spotlights.name: Kilanji
spotlights.spot_it: Thin, soft white crepes folded in a dish and soaked with coconut milk, banana and jaggery syrup.
spotlights.story_md: **Kilanji** is a thin crepe made from **rice flour and egg**, cooked quickly on a flat pan. It is served drenched in a sweet sauce of **coconut milk, mashed banana and jaggery**, so it is part pancake, part pudding. Families make it for festivals and for guests, especially during **Ramadan** and Eid. It shows how island cooks built sweets from the few things always at hand: rice from the ships, eggs from the backyard hens, and coconut from the palms.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the dish islanders most often name as their own.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pancake that drowns on purpose.

spotlights.name: Octopus fry
spotlights.spot_it: Chunks of octopus tentacle fried dark red with chilli and spices, chewy and smoky.
spotlights.story_md: On the reef flats at low tide, islanders wade out with a hooked stick and pull **octopus** from holes in the coral. The **day octopus** of these reefs hunts crabs by daylight and changes colour and skin texture in a blink to hide. Cleaned, beaten to tenderise, and fried with **chilli, pepper, garlic and coconut oil**, it becomes one of the islands' favourite dishes, served at weddings and to visitors. Tourism menus put **fried octopus** alongside tuna as a must-try.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is food gathered on foot from the reef, a skill most children learn.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hunted at low tide with a stick, eaten at dinner with chilli.

spotlights.name: Dweep halwa
spotlights.spot_it: Small dark-brown balls or blocks of a sticky sweet made from coconut and coconut jaggery.
spotlights.story_md: Islanders make a sweet called **dweep halwa** or **dweep unda** ('island ball') from coconut and the dark **jaggery** boiled down from **coconut sap**. The sap is collected by climbers who cut the flower stalk of the palm and hang a pot under it; fresh, it is a sweet drink called **neera**; boiled for hours, it thickens to syrup and then to jaggery. The halwa keeps for weeks, and islanders take it to relatives on the mainland as a gift.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns the palm's sap, not just its nuts, into food.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sweet tapped from a flower stalk.

spotlights.name: Breadfruit (state tree)
spotlights.spot_it: A green, bumpy fruit the size of a football hanging from a large-leaved tree.
spotlights.story_md: The **breadfruit**, *Artocarpus*, is Lakshadweep's state tree. Its fruit is starchy rather than sweet, and island cooks treat it like a potato: sliced and fried as chips, boiled and mashed with coconut, or cooked in curries. One tree can give **hundreds of fruits a year**, which made breadfruit a famine food across tropical islands. It was the cargo of the **HMS Bounty** in 1789, when Britain wanted to ship breadfruit from Tahiti to feed enslaved workers in the Caribbean, and the crew mutinied.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rare staple that grows well on coral islands.
spotlights.memory_hook: The fruit the Bounty mutineers threw overboard.

sections.title: How the islands earn and stay connected
sections.intro_md:
Lakshadweep's economy is small and leans on the government. The big public employers are the Administration, schools, hospitals and the shipping and power departments. Private income comes from three things: **fish, coconut and tourists**.

The sea gives about **21,000 tonnes** of fish a year, about **60% of it tuna**, almost all **skipjack and yellowfin**, caught by the old **pole-and-line** method. The land gives coconuts on nearly every square metre; there are only **2.58 hectares** of other farmland. The government runs **five coir factories** and a **tuna canning factory**.

Everything else depends on links to the mainland. Seven passenger ships run from **Kochi**, taking **14 to 20 hours**. There is one airport, at **Agatti**, with a short runway for small turboprops. Power came from **diesel** generators, now topped up by **solar** plants, and drinking water partly from plants that use the cold of the deep sea. In **January 2024** an undersea **fibre-optic cable** from Kochi finally gave the islands fast internet.

spotlights.name: Pole-and-line tuna fishing
spotlights.spot_it: A crew standing at the back of a boat, flicking tuna one by one out of a boiling patch of sea with short bamboo poles.
spotlights.story_md: Island fishermen first net small **live bait fish** in the lagoon at dawn and keep them in a tank on deck. At sea they find a tuna shoal, throw handfuls of bait overboard and **spray water** on the surface so it looks like a feeding frenzy. The tuna strike at anything. Men standing at the stern swing **barbless hooks** on short poles into the water and flick each fish over their shoulder onto the deck in one move. A good crew can land **hundreds** of fish in a few hours. Because each fish is caught singly, there is almost **no bycatch** of turtles, sharks or dolphins.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the most selective ways to catch tuna in the world.
spotlights.memory_hook: One fish, one flick, no nets.

spotlights.name: Coir
spotlights.spot_it: Brown, bristly rope and mats made from the hairy husk of the coconut.
spotlights.story_md: Coir is the fibre from the outer **husk of the coconut**. Islanders soak the husks in lagoon pits for months, beat out the fibre, and twist it into **yarn and rope**. For centuries this was the islands' main export: the **Portuguese** came in the late 15th century for coir to rig their ships, and the **Arakkal** rulers made it a monopoly. **Chetlat** was known for coir as good as the best of the other islands. Today the Administration runs **five coir factories**, **five production and demonstration centres** and **seven curling units** making fibre, yarn and mats.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the trade that drew empires to the islands.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Portuguese came for rope, not spice.

spotlights.name: The ship to Kochi
spotlights.spot_it: A white passenger ship anchored off the reef while small boats ferry people and sacks of rice to the jetty.
spotlights.story_md: For most islanders the mainland is a ship away. In **2023** seven passenger vessels ran between **Kochi** and the islands, taking **14 to 20 hours**. Big ships cannot cross most reefs, so they anchor outside, and passengers and cargo come in by small boat or barge. In the monsoon, from about **May to September**, seas are rough, sailings drop, and the islands live on stored supplies. When ships are out for repair, as happened repeatedly in **2023 and 2024**, tickets become a political issue. The government plans new ports at **Andrott, Kalpeni and Kadmat** under the Sagarmala programme.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the islands' lifeline for food, fuel, hospitals and exams.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty hours to the mainland, if the ship is running.

spotlights.name: Making water from the cold deep sea
spotlights.spot_it: A plant on the shore with a long pipe running out past the reef into deep water.
spotlights.story_md: Fresh water on a coral island is scarce: just a thin lens of rainwater under the sand. In **2005** India's **National Institute of Ocean Technology** opened the world's first **low-temperature thermal desalination** plant at **Kavaratti**. It works by lowering the air pressure so that warm surface sea water **boils at about room temperature**; the vapour is then condensed into fresh water using cold water pumped from deep below, at **7 to 15 °C**. The Kavaratti plant was built to make about **100,000 litres a day**, and similar plants followed on other islands.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is an Indian invention designed for exactly this kind of place.
spotlights.memory_hook: Warm sea water boils in a vacuum, cold sea water condenses it.

spotlights.name: Agatti airport
spotlights.spot_it: A single grey strip filling the southern tip of a narrow island, with water on three sides.
spotlights.story_md: Lakshadweep's only airport opened on **16 April 1988**, built for small **Dornier 228** planes. Its runway is about **1.2 km** long and occupies much of the island's southern end, so take-offs feel like launching off an aircraft carrier. Flights from **Kochi** take about **1.5 hours**. Passenger numbers jumped after the 2024 publicity: **47,266** in 2023 to 24, **117,409** in 2024 to 25 and **136,680** in 2025 to 26. In **July 2024** the government approved extending the runway over the lagoon and making Agatti a dual civil and military airfield.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the territory's front door and its tourism bottleneck.
spotlights.memory_hook: An island where the runway is longer than the island is wide.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Lakshadweep's population is smaller than a large town's, so a handful of people loom large. Its politics has been dominated by **one family and one rival**: **P. M. Sayeed**, who held the Lok Sabha seat for **37 years**, his son **Hamdullah Sayeed**, and **Mohammed Faizal**, who beat the son twice. Seats are won by margins of a few hundred votes; in 2004 the elder Sayeed lost by **71**.

Since there is no elected assembly, the most powerful person in the islands is often the **Administrator**, appointed from Delhi. The current one, **Praful Khoda Patel**, has been the most controversial in the territory's history.

And then there are islanders who became known far beyond the islands, like **Ali Manikfan** of Minicoy, a self-taught naturalist and boat builder with a fish named after him.

spotlights.name: P. M. Sayeed
spotlights.spot_it: A smiling politician in white with a moustache, often pictured in the Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker's chair.
spotlights.story_md: **Padanatha Mohammed Sayeed**, born on **Andrott** in **1941**, was elected to the Lok Sabha at **26** in **1967** as an independent, then joined Congress, and won **ten elections in a row**, holding the seat until **2004**: nearly **37 years**, among the longest unbroken runs of any Indian MP. He was **Deputy Speaker** of the Lok Sabha from **1998 to 2004** and a minister several times. In 2004 he lost by just **71 votes**, moved to the Rajya Sabha, and became **Union Power Minister**. He died in **Seoul** in **December 2005**. A seabird reserve in the islands carries his name.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He put a territory of 60,000 people into national politics for four decades.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten wins in a row, then lost by 71 votes.

spotlights.name: Muhammed Hamdullah Sayeed
spotlights.spot_it: A younger, bearded Congress MP in white, son of P. M. Sayeed.
spotlights.story_md: **Muhammed Hamdullah Sayeed** won his father's old seat for Congress in **2009**, lost it to Mohammed Faizal in **2014** and again by just **823 votes** in **2019**. In **June 2024** he won it back, beating Faizal by **2,647 votes** with **52.3%** of the vote on a turnout of **85%**. He has opposed several of the Administration's plans, including proposals to take over land for defence and tourism projects, positioning himself as the islanders' voice against decisions made in Delhi.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He carries the islands' leading political family into the 2020s.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lost by 823, won by 2,647: Lakshadweep elections are decided by a ferry-load.

spotlights.name: Mohammed Faizal
spotlights.spot_it: A Nationalist Congress Party politician who twice lost and twice regained his seat in the same term.
spotlights.story_md: **Mohammed Faizal** of the NCP won Lakshadweep in **2014** and **2019**. In **January 2023** a Kavaratti court sentenced him to **ten years** for attempted murder in a clash during the **2009** election, and he was disqualified from the Lok Sabha. Days later the **Kerala High Court suspended** the conviction, the Election Commission put off the by-election, and on **29 March 2023** his membership was restored. In **2024** he lost to Hamdullah Sayeed. His case became a national test of how quickly courts and Parliament act when a sitting MP is convicted.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His story shows how small-island politics can reach the Supreme Court and Parliament.
spotlights.memory_hook: Disqualified in January, restored in March, defeated in June of the next year.

spotlights.name: Praful Khoda Patel
spotlights.spot_it: A Gujarat politician turned administrator, the face of the 2021 'Save Lakshadweep' protests.
spotlights.story_md: **Praful Khoda Patel**, a former Gujarat minister of state for home, took charge of Lakshadweep on **5 December 2020** after the previous Administrator died. Within months his administration ended quarantine rules for arrivals, closed government **dairy farms**, took **meat out of school meals**, proposed a **beef ban**, a preventive detention law, a **two-child rule** for panchayat candidates and a **development authority** with wide powers over land. Islanders, Kerala's parties and the territory's own BJP members protested; Kerala's assembly passed a resolution seeking his recall. His supporters say he is bringing investment and tourism to a neglected territory.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned the islands' governance into a national debate.
spotlights.memory_hook: One administrator, one 'Save Lakshadweep' hashtag.

spotlights.name: Ali Manikfan
spotlights.spot_it: An old man with a white beard from Minicoy, polymath and boat builder, Padma Shri 2021.
spotlights.story_md: **Ali Manikfan** left school young and taught himself marine biology, astronomy, boat building and languages. Working with the **Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute** in the 1960s, he found a new reef fish, which scientists named ***Abudefduf manikfani*** after him. In **1980 to 1981**, explorer **Tim Severin** hired him to lead the building of the ***Sohar***, a 27-metre Arab trading ship sewn together **without a single metal nail**, which then sailed about **9,600 km from Oman to China**. Manikfan also built a motorised bicycle and rode it from Tamil Nadu to Delhi. He received the **Padma Shri** in **2021**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the islands' best-known example of self-taught genius.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fish, a nail-free ship and a bicycle motor, all from one Minicoy man.

spotlights.name: Leela Dube
spotlights.spot_it: An Indian anthropologist whose book on Kalpeni is still the standard account of island family life.
spotlights.story_md: **Leela Dube** (1923 to 2012) was one of India's leading anthropologists of kinship and gender. Her book ***Matriliny and Islam: Religion and Society in the Laccadives*** came out of fieldwork on **Kalpeni**. She showed how islanders held together two systems that are often thought to clash: a **matrilineal** family in which property and identity pass through women, and **Islamic law**, which gives sons larger shares than daughters. The islanders' answer was to keep two kinds of property, one for each system. Her work is still the starting point for anyone writing about Lakshadweep society.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She explained to the rest of India how the islands' families actually work.
spotlights.memory_hook: The scholar who found two inheritance laws in one family.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Getting to Lakshadweep takes paperwork. Every visitor who is not a native islander, Indians included, needs an **entry permit** from the Administration, and the permit needs a confirmed place to stay. Foreign tourists are allowed only on some islands. The season runs from about **October to mid May**; the monsoon closes most water sports.

Tourism began in **1974**, when **Bangaram** opened to international visitors. In 2018 the islands had about **10,400 Indian and 1,300 foreign** tourists. Most come for the water: snorkelling and diving on reef walls, kayaking across lagoons, glass-bottomed boats for those who do not swim. The government tourism company **SPORTS** runs resorts and a ship package that cruises between islands.

Bring cash, expect little nightlife, and remember that the inhabited islands are conservative Muslim communities: swimwear belongs on the resort beach, not in the village.

spotlights.name: Bangaram
spotlights.spot_it: A teardrop island ringed with white sand inside a huge pale lagoon, with almost no buildings.
spotlights.story_md: **Bangaram** is a teardrop island of **0.62 km²** inside an atoll whose lagoon covers about **36 km²**. Its resort opened in **1974**, the start of tourism in Lakshadweep, with **60 cottages** and no permanent village. It is the **only place in the territory where alcohol is allowed**. The atoll also has **Thinnakara**, where islanders from Agatti run beach huts, and the shrinking **Parali** islets. Bangaram is reached by boat from Agatti, about **7 km** away. Its quiet, its brackish central pond and its sea birds have made it the islands' best-known postcard.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where Lakshadweep's tourism started and the model for every plan since.
spotlights.memory_hook: The only island in Lakshadweep where you can order a beer.

spotlights.name: Kadmat
spotlights.spot_it: A long, thin island, about 9 km by half a kilometre, with a shallow lagoon along its whole western side.
spotlights.story_md: **Kadmat** is a ribbon of land about **9.3 km long** and barely **0.57 km wide**, with a shallow western lagoon only **2 to 3 m** deep. It had **5,389 people** in 2011 in a single village. Its **Water Sports Institute**, opened in **1998**, and a dive centre make it the islands' main place to learn scuba diving. Four turtle species, green, hawksbill, olive ridley and leatherback, are reported here, and green turtles nest on its beaches. In **2024** the Tata group's IHCL announced a **Taj** resort for Kadmat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the place to learn to dive in Indian waters.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nine kilometres long, half a kilometre wide, all of it lagoon-front.

spotlights.name: Agatti
spotlights.spot_it: Where every flight lands: a slim island of palms, a fishing harbour on the lagoon side and a long white beach.
spotlights.story_md: **Agatti** is **7.6 km long** and only about **0.85 km wide**, with **7,560 people** in 2011 and a lagoon of about **25 km²**. Everyone who flies in lands here, and many visitors base themselves on the island and take boats to Bangaram, Thinnakara and the reefs. Agatti is also a **fishing** island, with a big tuna boat fleet and drying yards. Highlights include **Anthan beach** and the reefs off its southern tip, where turtles graze in the seagrass.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the territory's air gateway and a working fishing island.
spotlights.memory_hook: Land, then walk to the beach; the airport and the lagoon share an island.

spotlights.name: Kalpeni's lagoon islets
spotlights.spot_it: Small uninhabited islets in a shallow lagoon, reached by kayak from Koomel beach.
spotlights.story_md: Kalpeni's lagoon is studded with islets: **Cheriyam** to the north, the **Tilakkam** group and tiny **Pitti** in the west. From **Koomel beach**, visitors kayak or wade across the shallow lagoon to snorkel over coral gardens around the islets. Kalpeni's **37-metre lighthouse** gives a view over the whole atoll, and the storm bank of coral rubble from **1847** is a strange sight along the eastern shore. Village troupes perform **Kolkali and Parichakali** for visitors on the beach.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It offers the best mix of lagoon, reef and village in one atoll.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kayak to an island you can walk around in five minutes.

spotlights.name: Suheli Par
spotlights.when: Seasonal fishing camps, October to April
spotlights.spot_it: Two palm-covered islets on the rim of a big oval lagoon, with no village, only fishermen's huts in season.
spotlights.story_md: **Suheli Par** is an oval atoll about **17 km long** with a lagoon of about **88 km²** and three bits of land: **Valiyakara**, with a lighthouse, **Cheriyakara**, and a sandbank. Nobody lives there permanently. From **mid October to mid April**, fishermen from **Agatti and Kavaratti** camp on Cheriyakara to catch and dry tuna. Its rich reefs led to proposals to make it a **marine national park**. In **2024**, IHCL announced a **Taj** resort here too, which conservationists watch closely.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the territory's wildest atoll and the next frontier for luxury tourism.
spotlights.memory_hook: A fishing camp today, a Taj resort tomorrow, if plans hold.

sections.title: What is happening now (2021 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Lakshadweep has had a louder five years than at any time since 1956. The arguments are about who decides the islands' future: islanders, who want land rules and ways of life protected, or Delhi, which sees a strategic outpost and a tourism opportunity.

**2021:** a set of draft regulations from the new Administrator set off the **'Save Lakshadweep'** protests. **2023:** the MP is convicted, disqualified and restored within weeks. **January 2024:** the Prime Minister's visit, the undersea cable and the Maldives row. **March 2024:** a new naval base, **INS Jatayu**, on Minicoy. **July 2024:** approval for a military airfield on Minicoy and a bigger Agatti airport. **2024:** global coral bleaching hits the reefs again. **July 2025:** a proposal to take over **Bitra** island for defence use. **2025 to 26:** Agatti handles a record **136,680** passengers, and new airlines announce routes, including a Bengaluru service from **November 2026**.

Behind the headlines, the basic problems remain: unreliable ships, rising seas, and how to grow tourism without breaking reefs and communities that have little land to spare.

spotlights.name: Save Lakshadweep, 2021
spotlights.spot_it: Islanders holding placards on their rooftops and in the sea, because covid rules banned gatherings.
spotlights.story_md: In **2021** the Administration published draft rules that islanders saw as an attack on their land and way of life: the **Lakshadweep Development Authority Regulation**, giving power to plan and acquire land; a **preventive detention** law in a territory with very little crime; a **beef ban**; and a **two-child limit** for panchayat candidates. With covid restrictions on gatherings, protesters held up placards in their homes and in the lagoon. Kerala's assembly sought Patel's recall. A Lakshadweep filmmaker, **Aisha Sultana**, was booked for **sedition** after calling the policies a 'bio-weapon' on TV, and got anticipatory bail from the Kerala High Court.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made the islands' relationship with Delhi a national political issue.
spotlights.memory_hook: A protest held standing in the sea.

spotlights.name: INS Jatayu, Minicoy
spotlights.spot_it: A small naval base by Minicoy's jetty, watching the Nine and Eight Degree Channels.
spotlights.story_md: The Navy has had a small detachment on Minicoy since the **early 1980s**. On **6 March 2024** it became a full base, **INS Jatayu**, the second in Lakshadweep after **INS Dweeprakshak** at Kavaratti (2012). Its job is to watch the **Eight and Nine Degree Channels**, two of the busiest shipping lanes between the Gulf, Europe and East Asia, and to counter **piracy** and **drug smuggling**. In **July 2024** the government approved a new **air base** on Minicoy for fighters, transport planes and drones, with a civilian enclave; construction was under way by late 2025. Its timing, months after the Maldives asked Indian troops to leave, was noticed in Male.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns the territory into India's forward post in the Arabian Sea.
spotlights.memory_hook: A naval base 125 km from the Maldives, opened the year Indian troops left it.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
**Myth: Sardar Patel won Lakshadweep in a race with Pakistan in 1947.** A popular story says Pakistan sent a ship to claim the Muslim-majority islands and an Indian warship got there first and raised the flag. It appears in speeches and on social media, but historians have found **no documents** showing a Pakistani attempt; the islands were part of the Madras Presidency and passed to India as a matter of course.

**Myth: Lakshadweep is part of Kerala.** It is a separate **union territory**, run from Delhi through an Administrator. The link to Kerala is cultural, linguistic and legal: its appeals go to the **Kerala High Court**.

**Myth: Anyone can buy a beach plot.** Land transfer to people who are not islanders is tightly restricted, and even Indian visitors need an **entry permit**.

**Myth: It is 'India's Maldives' and just like it.** Both sit on the same ridge, but the Maldives has about **1,190 islands** and over 500,000 people; Lakshadweep has 36 and about 65,000. Only Minicoy shares the Maldivian language.

**Fact that sounds like a myth: an island vanished.** Parali I in Bangaram atoll was **washed away by 2017**.

sections.title: Recap: Lakshadweep in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. India's smallest UT: **32.62 km²** of land, **36 islands**, **10 inhabited**, about **4,200 km²** of lagoon.
2. **64,473** people in 2011; **96.6% Muslim**; nearly all **Scheduled Tribes**.
3. Islands are **coral atolls** on the **Chagos-Laccadive Ridge**, mostly **1 to 2 m** above the sea.
4. History: **Cholas** (1018), **Arakkal** rulers of Kannur, **Tipu** (1787), **British** (1799 and 1908), **UT in 1956**, renamed **1973**.
5. **Minicoy** speaks **Dhivehi**, writes **Thaana**, and is 125 km from the Maldives; its lighthouse dates from **1885**.
6. Families are **matrilineal**; husbands traditionally **visited** at night.
7. Dances: **Kolkali, Parichakali, Lava, Oppana**.
8. Food: **tuna** (dried as **mas**), **coconut**, octopus, kilanji.
9. Economy: **pole-and-line tuna**, coir, tourism; one airport at **Agatti** (1988).
10. Now: **2021 protests**, **2024** Modi visit and Maldives row, **INS Jatayu**, Minicoy air base, the **Bitra** proposal.

best_facts.fact: Lakshadweep has 32.6 km² of land but about 4,200 km² of lagoon and an economic zone of about 400,000 km², roughly a fifth of India's.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's smallest territory controls one of its biggest pieces of sea.

best_facts.fact: After Modi posted Lakshadweep holiday photos in January 2024, three Maldivian deputy ministers who mocked them were suspended, and Indian arrivals in the Maldives fell 42% over the next four months.
best_facts.why_surprising: Beach photos caused a diplomatic incident.

best_facts.fact: In traditional island families a husband stayed in his mother's house and visited his wife only at night, and ancestral property passed from mother to daughter, among a population that is 97% Muslim.
best_facts.why_surprising: Matriliny and Islam coexist in the same family.

best_facts.fact: The name Minicoy comes from a British official's mistake: an islander who worked in the Nicobars, which Minicoy sailors called Minikaa-raajje, gave both place names, and 'Minikaa' was written down.
best_facts.why_surprising: An island named after another island 2,000 km away.

best_facts.fact: An islet of Bangaram atoll, Parali I, had been completely washed away by 2017; its neighbour Parali II had lost about 80% of its area.
best_facts.why_surprising: An Indian island disappeared in living memory.

best_facts.fact: In 2020 Lakshadweep got the world's first protected area set up specifically for sea cucumbers, which sell dried for up to about USD 1,000 a kilo.
best_facts.why_surprising: A global first for an animal most people have never seen.

best_facts.fact: Sooty terns, the state bird, cannot float because their feathers lack oil, so young birds stay on the wing for 3 to 10 years before landing to breed.
best_facts.why_surprising: A seabird that never rests on the sea.

best_facts.fact: P. M. Sayeed won the Lakshadweep seat ten times in a row from 1967, then lost it in 2004 by 71 votes.
best_facts.why_surprising: Thirty-seven years undone by a few families.

best_facts.fact: Kavaratti hosted the world's first low-temperature thermal desalination plant in 2005, boiling sea water at about room temperature in a vacuum and condensing it with cold water from the deep.
best_facts.why_surprising: An Indian island pioneered a new way to make drinking water.

best_facts.fact: Bitra, the smallest inhabited island at 0.18 km², had no permanent residents until 1945, when a woman from Chetlat settled there.
best_facts.why_surprising: One woman founded a whole island community.

best_facts.fact: Ali Manikfan of Minicoy, who left school early, has a reef fish named after him and led the building of the Sohar, a 27 m Arab ship sewn without metal that sailed from Oman to China.
best_facts.why_surprising: A self-taught islander at the centre of a famous voyage.

best_facts.fact: The Minicoy lighthouse was built in 1885 with bricks shipped from London and run from Colombo; India's flag went up on it only on 2 April 1956.
best_facts.why_surprising: Part of India was run from Ceylon until 1956.

best_facts.fact: Thaana, the script of Minicoy's Dhivehi, built its first nine letters from Arabic numerals.
Bangaram is the only island in Lakshadweep where alcohol is allowed.

side_dish.title: How Darwin explained atolls before anyone could see one sink
side_dish.body_md:
In **1836**, on the voyage of HMS Beagle, the young **Charles Darwin** stood on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands in the Indian Ocean and puzzled over a question sailors had asked for centuries: why do coral islands form **rings** around lagoons, in the middle of deep ocean, when reef-building corals can only grow in the top few tens of metres of sunlit water?

His answer, published in **1842**, was bold. Start with a volcanic island with a **fringing reef** around its shore. Let the island **slowly sink**, as the sea floor cools and sags. The coral keeps growing upward to stay in the light, so the reef holds its place at the surface while the land shrinks inside it. First you get a **barrier reef** with a lagoon between it and the island. When the last peak goes under, only the ring is left: an **atoll**.

He could not prove it. Proof needed a drill. In the early **1950s**, American geologists drilled into **Enewetak** atoll in the Pacific. They went through more than a kilometre of coral limestone, all of it laid down in shallow water, and hit **volcanic basalt** at about **1,400 metres**. The island had sunk, the coral had kept pace, exactly as Darwin said.

Lakshadweep's atolls tell the same story on top of the **Chagos-Laccadive Ridge**. The catch today is speed: corals can keep up with slow sinking, but they need to be healthy to keep up with **rising seas**.

offline_task.title: Cook an island-style tuna and coconut stir fry
offline_task.body_md:
Make a simple version of **mas podichathu** tonight.

**You need (serves 2):** one 150 to 185 g tin of tuna in brine, drained (or 200 g fresh tuna, boiled for 10 minutes and flaked); 1 cup grated coconut (fresh or frozen); 1 small onion, finely chopped; 3 cloves garlic, crushed; 1 or 2 green chillies, chopped; a sprig of curry leaves; half a teaspoon of turmeric; half a teaspoon of chilli powder; 2 tablespoons coconut oil; salt.

**Method:** heat the oil, fry the curry leaves for a few seconds, then add onion, garlic and chilli and cook until soft. Add turmeric and chilli powder, stir for 30 seconds, then add the tuna, breaking it into fine flakes. Add the coconut and keep stirring on medium heat for **8 to 10 minutes**, until the mix is dry, golden and smells toasted. Salt to taste.

Eat it with rice or chapati. For a Maldivian twist, skip the cooking: mix the tuna, coconut, raw onion, chilli and lime juice and eat it with flatbread, which is **mas huni**. Notice how the coconut and fish blur together; that is the taste of an island where both come from the same few metres of shore.
